qs.q: A 65‑year‑old man with a pancreatic head tumor has a prolonged prothrombin time and INR due to obstructive jaundice. Which immediate intervention best corrects this coagulopathy before any invasive procedure?
o: Administer a single dose of vitamin K intravenously
Transfuse fresh‑frozen plasma to replace clotting factors
Place a biliary stent endoscopically to relieve obstruction
qs.e: Vitamin K deficiency from cholestasis prolongs PT/INR and is rapidly corrected by giving vitamin K. Fresh‑frozen plasma would only temporarily replace clotting factors without addressing the underlying deficiency.
qs.s: Pancreatic Head Cancer and Periampullary Tumours: Whipple Procedure: MCQs

qs.q: A 52-year-old man with obstructive jaundice secondary to malignant biliary obstruction has a prolonged prothrombin time. Which of the following interventions best differentiates this from hepatocellular synthetic failure?
o: A. Measurement of serum CA 19-9 tumour markers
B. Performance of diagnostic endoscopic cholangiopancreatography
C. Analysis of urine urobilinogen concentration levels
D. Administration of parenteral vitamin K replacement therapy
qs.e: Obstructive jaundice impairs the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins including vitamin K, causing a prolonged prothrombin time that is successfully corrected with vitamin K administration. In hepatocellular failure, the synthetic defect does not correct with vitamin K.

es.q: A patient presents with an isolated elevation of Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP) and significantly prolonged Prothrombin Time (PT) with low albumin. Interpret these findings in the context of liver function tests.
es.m: Isolated elevation of Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP) suggests cholestasis or biliary obstruction (2 marks). A significantly prolonged Prothrombin Time (PT) and low albumin indicate severe hepatocellular synthetic dysfunction. This implies the liver's ability to produce clotting factors (measured by PT) and albumin is severely impaired. (3 marks)
es.s: Liver Histology, Physiology and Pathology — Practice Questions

es.q: A liver biopsy from a deceased patient shows severe hepatocellular dysfunction. The post-mortem lab results indicate low serum albumin and a prolonged prothrombin time (PT). Explain the significance of these findings in the context of hepatocyte synthetic function and state why ALT is generally cons
es.m: Low albumin and prolonged PT indicate severe impairment of hepatocyte synthetic function. Albumin is synthesized by hepatocytes, and a low level reflects reduced synthesis. Prothrombin time measures the activity of clotting factors, which are also synthesized by the liver, and a prolonged PT signifies impaired production. ALT (SGPT) is considered more specific for liver injury than AST (SGOT) because ALT is predominantly found in the liver, while AST is also present in other tissues like cardiac muscle and skeletal muscle.

exam: How would you differentiate vitamin K deficiency from liver disease when PT is prolonged? — Check albumin, bilirubin, liver ultrasound; a normal aPTT and normal fibrinogen favour vitamin K deficiency.

A patient with chronic hepatitis B has an INR of 1.8. What is the clinical significance? — Indicates moderate synthetic dysfunction; monitor for bleeding, consider antiviral therapy and avoid hepatotoxic drugs.
Why is a normal aPTT helpful in a prolonged PT case? — It suggests the intrinsic pathway is intact, pointing to extrinsic pathway defects or vitamin K deficiency rather than DIC.
What is the rationale for giving fresh frozen plasma in a patient with PT 3.0 who is bleeding? — FFP supplies all clotting factors, rapidly correcting coagulopathy.
In a resource‑poor setting, a patient with jaundice and bruising has a prolonged PT. What is the most likely cause? — Chronic liver disease (e.g., hepatitis B/C or schistosomiasis).
ai.title: Prolonged Prothrombin Time
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Prolonged PT indicates impaired synthesis of vitamin‑K dependent clotting factors, usually from liver disease, vitamin K deficiency or anticoagulant therapy. It signals bleeding risk and guides urgent management.

sections.p: PT measures the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways. An INR >1.2 (or PT >14 s in a normal population) is considered prolonged. Diagnosis requires a repeat test to exclude lab error and correlation with clinical context.

t.b: Is clotting time longer than normal? A prolonged result suggests factor deficiency or anticoagulant effect.

sections.p: Severity is graded by INR: 1.2‑1.5 mild, 1.6‑2.0 moderate, >2.0 severe. Clinical staging parallels liver disease (Child‑Pugh A/B/C) when PT is a surrogate for synthetic function.

In low‑resource settings the top causes are chronic liver disease (viral hepatitis B/C, schistosomiasis, alcohol), vitamin K deficiency (poor diet, malabsorption, broad‑spectrum antibiotics), and warfarin or other anticoagulants. Less common: inherited factor deficiencies, sepsis‑induced DIC, severe malnutrition.

t.b: Is synthetic liver function impaired? Low albumin supports liver disease.

t.a: History of antibiotics or herbal remedies
t.b: Do they cause vitamin K antagonism?

sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic or present with bruising, mucosal bleeding, or spontaneous haemorrhage (e.g., intracranial). In liver disease, associated jaundice, ascites, encephalopathy, and hypoalbuminaemia are common.

Confirm PT/INR, repeat to rule out lab error. Complementary tests: PT, aPTT, fibrinogen, platelets, liver function tests, viral serology, ultrasound for liver pathology, and vitamin K level if available.

t.b: Is the intrinsic pathway also affected? A normal aPTT with prolonged PT points to extrinsic pathway or vitamin K deficiency.
Is there consumption coagulopathy? Low fibrinogen suggests DIC.
Does it show cirrhosis or focal lesions?

sections.p: Urgent bleeding (intracranial, gastrointestinal, retroperitoneal), severe thrombocytopenia, or rapidly rising INR (>3) with clinical bleeding require immediate intervention.
Re‑check INR weekly until stable, then monthly. Counsel on diet, avoid hepatotoxic drugs, screen for hepatitis, and educate on safe use of herbal remedies.

PT can be falsely normal if the patient is on low‑dose warfarin or has early liver disease. Vitamin K levels may be normal despite functional deficiency due to impaired hepatic uptake.
